note.question: What determines innovations embody novel features or cutting-edge components aimed at delivering desired customer benefits?
note.overview: Innovations embody novel features or cutting-edge components aimed at delivering desired customer benefits. Oftentimes, however, we observe the need to recall new products shortly after their introduction. Indeed, a firm may rush an innovation to market in an attempt to pre-empt rivals and capture early demand, yet in so doing forgo rigorous testing, thus subjecting itself to the risk of a product recall.

source.quote: Indeed, a firm may rush an innovation to market in an attempt to pre-empt rivals and capture early demand, yet in so doing forgo rigorous testing, thus subjecting itself to the risk of a product recall.

The results further demonstrate how firms’ desire to forgo testing exhibits an inverse-U pattern as consumers become more heterogeneous and how competitive forces may induce both firms to forgo testing, although the resulting profits are lower than had they both committed to conduct testing.

source.section: I Don’t “Recall”: The Decision to Delay Innovation Launch to Avoid Costly Product Failure
source.quote: Each ﬁrm must decide whether to conduct time-consuming quality assurance testing, which ensures no defects or safety problems but delays the launch.

Samsung estimated the direct cost of the recall at $5.3 billion; in a survey of its customers, 34% responded that they would be reluctant to purchase another phone from the brand; and the company’s stock price dropped by more than 8%, effectively removing $19 billion off its book value (Cuthbertson 2016).
